title: Indian-American House Strength Set to Fall From Six to Four After Midterms
excerpt: Krishnamoorthi and Thanedar lost their primaries, four incumbents are in safe seats, and only Amish Shah and Pia Dandiya can grow the caucus — the full Indian-origin roster for the November 3 elections, from Congress to city hall.
body:
• Indian-American representation in the US House is set to fall from six members to four after the November 3 midterms, because Raja Krishnamoorthi and Shri Thanedar both lost Democratic primaries earlier this year.
  • The four incumbents seeking re-election — Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam — are each in seats rated Solid or Safe Democratic; in two of those races their Republican opponent is also Indian American.
  • Only two newcomers can grow the caucus: Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st District and Pia Dandiya in Florida's 22nd, both in races rated Toss-up to Lean by forecasters.
  • For Indian-American voters: Election Day is November 3, early voting is already open in several states, and the 2026 AAPI survey found 66% of Asian Indian respondents preferring the Democratic House candidate to 18% for the Republican.

The number of Indian Americans in the US House of Representatives is expected to drop from six to four after the November 3 midterm elections, unless Democrats Amish Shah of Arizona or Pia Dandiya of Florida win their tight congressional races, according to Business Times reporting via IANS. This guide sets out the full roster — who is staying, who has already gone, and which races will decide the final count.

The two departures are already decided

The current six Indian-American House members, all Democrats and collectively known as the "Samosa Caucus," are Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Shri Thanedar and Suhas Subramanyam. Two of the six will not be in the next House regardless of what happens in November. Krishnamoorthi vacated his Illinois seat to run for the Senate and lost the March 17 Democratic primary to Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton, 40.39 per cent to 32.71 per cent. Thanedar lost the August 4 Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th District to state Representative Donavan McKinney, 51.9 per cent to 48.1 per cent, in a race where Justice Democrats invested nearly $1 million behind the challenger.

The four incumbents seeking re-election

Bera in California's 3rd District, Khanna in California's 17th, Jayapal in Washington's 7th and Subramanyam in Virginia's 10th are each contesting seats rated Solid or Safe Democratic. In two of those districts, the Republican challenger is also Indian American: Khanna faces Ritesh Tandon, and Jayapal faces Nirav Sheth. No Indian American has emerged as a competitive House nominee beyond this group, which caps how high the caucus count can go this cycle.

The two races that decide the count

In Arizona's 1st District, Shah, an emergency physician who narrowly lost the district in 2024, faces Trump-backed Republican Jay Feely. The Cook Political Report has shifted the race from Toss-up to Lean Democratic, while other forecasters still rate it a Toss-up; a recent poll put Shah at 44 per cent and Feely at 42 per cent, inside the margin of error. In Florida's redrawn 22nd District, an open seat, Dandiya faces Republican Casey Askar in a race rated between Toss-up and Lean Republican. Dandiya, born in Palm Beach County to Indian immigrant parents, would become Florida's first South Asian member of Congress if she wins.

"Obviously, this is not the result we sought… But unlike Donald Trump, I'm not going to question the outcome. I'm proud of the race we ran."

— Raja Krishnamoorthi, on his Senate primary defeat

Beyond the House: governor, attorney general, city hall

The congressional arithmetic is only part of the picture, as India Weekly's candidates-to-watch guide sets out. Vivek Ramaswamy is the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton, in a contest where recent polling has varied. In New York, Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging incumbent Attorney General Letitia James. In Maryland, Hyderabad-born Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller is seeking another term on the Democratic ticket with Governor Wes Moore. In Los Angeles, City Council member Nithya Raman is challenging Mayor Karen Bass in the November 3 runoff; a September UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and Los Angeles Times poll put Raman at 39 per cent and Bass at 28 per cent among likely voters, with 33 per cent undecided.

The electorate behind the candidates

Indian Americans number about 5.5 million people, roughly 1.6 per cent of the US population. The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey, released in August by AAPI Data and APIAVote, estimated 16 million AAPI voters eligible this year, including 1.6 million newly eligible since 2022, and found 90 per cent of registered AAPI voters planned to vote. Among Asian Indian respondents, 66 per cent preferred the Democratic candidate in House races and 18 per cent the Republican — a strong Democratic lean that coexists with prominent Republican candidacies such as Ramaswamy's and Komatireddy's. Cost of living and inflation were the leading concerns, cited as very or extremely important by 90 per cent of Asian-American respondents.

What November 3 will show

The floor for Indian-American House representation is now four. Whether it rises to five or six depends on two races forecasters cannot separate — Shah's in Arizona and Dandiya's in Florida. The wider test is whether representation built since Bera's first election in 2012 can be sustained when two senior members exit in the same cycle.
